https://hungarytoday.hu/house-speaker-ca.text: House Speaker Calls for International Cooperation to Protect Lake Balaton The Speaker of the National Assembly met with an EU commissioner in Balatonfüred. Ágnes Forsthoffer called for greater international cooperation and stronger water management efforts to protect the future of Lake Balaton, Világgazdaság reported. Speaker of the House Ágnes Forsthoffer met with EU Commissioner Jessika Roswall in Balatonfüred to discuss the future of Lake Balaton and water management in Hungary. According to the politician, the protection of natural waters knows no national borders, that is why international cooperation and a shared vision are necessary. Lake Balaton. Photo: MTI /Vasvári Tamás The Speaker of the House reported on her Facebook page that she met with the European Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience, and a Competitive Circular Economy at a professional conference held to mark World Lakes Day. At the event, Jessika Roswall outlined the key priorities of the European water resilience strategy and emphasized the importance of international cooperation. According to Forsthoffer, the issue of natural waters transcends political views, and their protection is only possible through joint action. At the event, experts, local government leaders, and representatives of professional and civil society organizations discussed the most important issues concerning Lake Balaton and water management. “As someone from the Lake Balaton region, it is a matter close to my heart to preserve the condition of our lakes and to take the necessary measures to ensure the responsible use and protection of our environment, livelihoods, and natural resources for the benefit of future generations,” said Forsthoffer, who was elected to parliament as a representative of the region. The program was organized by the Lake Balaton Development Council and the Balaton Integration Public Benefit Nonprofit Ltd. Due to the prolonged lack of rainfall and extreme heat, the condition of surface waters across the country is deteriorating dramatically: water levels on several rivers are near record lows, and some smaller lakes are already at risk of drying up. In addition to Lake Balaton, the water conditions of Lake Velence and several rivers in the Great Plain are also becoming increasingly unfavorable. Lake Velence. Photo: MTI /Vasvári Tamás The Balaton Association, which represents 92 municipalities, previously told Világgazdaság that it had contacted Speaker of the House Ágnes Forsthoffer regarding the future of Lake Balaton. The Speaker indicated that she would consult with the association, but this has not yet taken place. She has, however, already been in contact with other municipalities around Lake Balaton. Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor granted £302,000 for end of Royal Lodge lease Former prince surrendered lease on home within its first 25 years after public outcry about the rent he paid Jamie Grierson Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.39 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been granted £302,000 in compensation after the lease on his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor was officially surrendered. A crown estate spokesperson said the former prince paid £1.8m in repair and restoration costs, and the lease was handed back more than 50 years early. Andrew was entitled to compensation because, as per the terms of his lease, he surrendered it within the first 25 years. The crown estate spokesperson said: “The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return.” The former Duke of York moved out of the Windsor mansion this year as the US Department of Justice released files related to the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein . He was forced to move into Marsh Farm on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, amid public outcry about the rent he paid on the Royal Lodge. In June, a National Audit Office investigation revealed that the late queen’s second son received an unknown amount of private income from subletting three cottages on the Royal Lodge estate while paying a peppercorn rent – a small, symbolic payment – for more than two decades. The crown estate spokesperson said the property would now be marketed by two nationally recognised agents for its proposed future use. On Thursday, Mountbatten-Windsor won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him. The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants. Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful. The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation. The arrest followed information that emerged from the Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender. Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized. Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein. Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review .
